title: Uncovering Steady State Executions in Java Microbenchmarking with Call Graph Analysis
abstract_source: ICPE Companion PDF reviewed; abstract paraphrased for this catalog.
description: The paper uses sampled call graphs and machine learning to distinguish warmup from steady-state executions in Java microbenchmarks.

summary.core_contribution: The paper uses sampled call graphs and machine learning to distinguish warmup from steady-state executions in Java microbenchmarks.
summary.problem: JMH warmup and steady-state stages can differ structurally, while runtime-only detection gives little insight into why. The paper tests whether sampled call graphs distinguish the stages (pp. 1-2).
summary.method: Linux perf samples call stacks throughout JMH executions; timestamped start/end logs (Apache Log4j 2.11.2) delimit executions. Call graphs are visualized as flame graphs and embedded with Graph2Vec. PELT change-point detection supplies labels; this study checks 50 similar executions (5% of 1,000) after the change point rather than 500. MLP, Random Forest, Decision Tree, KNN, and SVC classifiers are evaluated (pp. 2-4).
summary.findings: The workload is a simple Java binary search with 10,000 executions across 10 forks on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 64-bit kernel 5.15.0-56, Perf 5.15.64, and JMH; warmup graphs have deeper/more irregular stacks and more interpreter functions. Accuracy/precision/recall: MLP 88.5/31.6/12.5%, RF 90.4/75.0/6%, DT 82.8/19.3/22.5%, KNN 89.8/45/9%, SVC 90/50/1% (pp. 3-4).
summary.limitations: Accuracy/precision are misleading without the very low recall; the paper attributes this partly to the small dataset/labels and possibly insufficient Graph2Vec vector size. Cross-JVM and cross-workload generalization are not established.
summary.future_work: More benchmarks, forks, and iterations; alternate/larger graph vectorizations; and unsupervised learning to avoid hand-derived labels (p. 4).
